lesson.title: ziehen & nehmen Dynasties
lesson.subtitle: Zug/umziehen/ausziehen; nehmen/nimmt/genommen — radiate each root into its family

hook.title: Two More Dynasties
hook.content: ziehen's family: der Zug (the pull — the train), der Aufzug (the up-pull — the elevator), der Umzug (the around-pull — moving house), umziehen (to move house), ausziehen (to move out), aufziehen (to raise). ziehen's English cousins are tow and tug — the train is named for pulling, just like the tugboat. nehmen's family: nehmen (take), nehmen's du/er forms — du nimmst, er nimmt (the vowel mutates!), nehmen's past nahm, participle genommen, and the separable mitnehmen (take along — you have drilled it since topic 15). Two roots, a dozen words, and every suffix law you own on display.

footnotes.title: nim in the Wild
footnotes.content: nehmen's true English twin is archaic nim 'to take' — which survives in nimble, 'quick to grasp'. English replaced nim with the Norse loan take; German never did. So nehmen/nimmst/genommen is the older English verb, still employed.

pattern.title: Radiate, Then Read
pattern.content: The ziehen radiation: ziehen, zog, gezogen (the a→o→o melody with an -en participle). Der Zug (train/pull/draught/move — a chess move is ein Zug!). Umziehen: Ich ziehe nach Berlin um — separable, prefix last. Der Umzug ist morgen (the move is tomorrow). The nehmen radiation: nehmen, nimmst/nimmt, nahm, genommen. Mitnehmen: Ich nehme das Essen mit (takeaway food!). And the stand-family cross-check: verstehen = understand, aufstehen = stand up — the same radiation English built with stand.
pattern.linguist_note: ziehen's -ogen participle (gezogen) marks it as a class-2 strong verb with an ancient -ug- suffix — the same class as English's lost 'towen'. The vowel melody a-o-o matches English's own old forms.

exercises.prompt: The ziehen dynasty — match each member with its meaning:
exercises.target_answer: der Zug, der Aufzug, der Umzug, umziehen, holen
exercises.meaning: the train, the elevator, moving house, to move, to fetch
exercises.explanation: One pulling root runs the entire transport-and-moving vocabulary — the way English 'draw' runs drawer, withdraw, drawback. holen joins the household: fetch-and-carry, no twin needed.

nehmen mutates in du/er: nimmst/nimmt — the i-mutation law you met in geben → gibt. The past nahm is a different note. mitnehmen mutates just like nehmen, and its prefix flies to the end: Er nimmt das Essen mit.

exercises.english_hint: ge + nomm + en — the past vowel changes again
exercises.explanation: nehmen, nahm, genommen — the vowel moves twice across the paradigm, exactly like come/came/come's family history.

exercises.prompt: Which English words are ziehen's true cousins?
options: tow and tug — the pulling family
exercises.target_answer: tow and tug — the pulling family
exercises.explanation: *teuhaną gave English tow/tug and German ziehen/der Zug. The train, the tugboat, and the tow-truck are one family.

nehmen mutates (nimmt) AND the separable prefix flies to the end — two laws in four words. Das Essen mitnehmen is literally 'to-go'. Wieder (again — wider's twin) fits any dynasty: holen — to fetch — stacks with it, das Essen wieder holen.

summary.outcome: Radiate ziehen and nehmen into their families with correct mutations and participles.
summary.takeaway: ziehen → Zug/Aufzug/Umzug (the tow/tug family); nehmen → nimmt/nahm/genommen (nim's living brother).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: sein, motion & the idiomatic mindset — ist↔is, war↔was, and Wie geht's = 'How goes it?'

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We tug / pull here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir ziehen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in ziehen & nehmen Dynasties.

ziehen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
ziehen.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, cognate with English tow / tug).

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

mitnehmen.context_translation: I want to take the food away / to go.

verstehen.etymology_derivation: Inseparable: ver- (for-) + stehen (stand). Past participle: verstanden (no ge-).

holen.context_phrase: Ich hole Wasser aus der Küche.
holen.context_translation: I am getting water from the kitchen.
holen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *holōną (to fetch); the page documents cognate English haul — the same hauling-and-fetching word. [wiktionary]

wieder.context_translation: We will see each other again.
wieder.etymology_derivation: Old High German widar 'against', from West Germanic *wiþr 'toward, against' — the page names English wither and widdershins as cognates; German wieder turned against into again. [wiktionary]

gewinnen.context_phrase: Unser Team will das Spiel gewinnen.
gewinnen.context_translation: Our team wants to win the game.
gewinnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *winnaną (PIE *wenh₁-) — English win descends from the same root (Old English winnan); strong verb: gewann, gewonnen. [wiktionary]

schauen.context_phrase: Wir schauen das Spiel im Fernsehen.
schauen.context_translation: We watch the game on TV.
schauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (to look); the page cites Old English scēawian and compares English show — the old look-verb that English turned into show. [wiktionary]

nuss.context_phrase: Der Kuchen hat Nüsse und Schokolade.
nuss.context_translation: The cake has nuts and chocolate.
nuss.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic hnuts; English nut is a direct cognate, with the Germanic t appearing as ss in German and the old initial h dropped. [wiktionary]

schmutzig.etymology_derivation: Schmutz (dirt) plus -ig; the entry says to compare English smutty, a word from the same Germanic family of dirty words with the same -y ending. [wiktionary]

kinn.context_phrase: Er hat einen kleinen Punkt am Kinn.
kinn.context_translation: He has a little spot on his chin.
kinn.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kinni, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from PIE *ǵénu- meaning jaw, cheek. English chin is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

adresse.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing from French adresse — the same French word that gives English address (ultimately Latin ad plus directum, made straight). [wiktionary]

geboren.context_translation: I was born in Berlin in 1990.
geboren.etymology_derivation: Past participle of gebären, a class 4 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *gaberaną, cognate with English bear; geboren matches the participle born of the same ablaut series. [wiktionary]

kokosnuss.context_translation: The coconut falls from the tree.
kokosnuss.etymology_derivation: Kokos + Nuss; the Nuss element is the documented twin of nut (t to ss), and Kokos is the same coco word that sits inside English coconut. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
